Imagine a boat sailing across a river. Everything is going smoothly — until the boat's hull scrapes against the sandy bottom and the boat gets stuck. It can no longer move. It has run aground.

Aground means: onto or on the ground at the bottom of a body of water, in a way that stops a vessel from moving.

It describes what happens when a ship, boat, or any floating vessel makes contact with — and gets stuck on — the shallow floor beneath the water. That floor could be sand, mud, rocks, a reef, or a sandbar.
How It Works as an Adverb

As an adverb, "aground" describes how or where something ends up. It almost always follows a verb — it tells you what happened to the vessel or what state it is now in.

The most common verb you'll see with it is run:

The ship ran aground near the coast.

This means the ship was moving, hit the shallow bottom, and got stuck there. The word "aground" here tells you where it ran and what happened as a result.

Other verbs commonly paired with "aground":

  • go aground — The fishing boat went aground in the fog.
  • be aground — The tanker is aground and cannot move.
  • lie aground — The old wreck has lain aground for decades.
  • sit aground — The barge sat aground until the tide came in.
Why It Matters: What "Aground" Actually Implies

When a vessel runs aground, a few things are always true:

  1. Part of the vessel is resting on solid ground — usually the hull (the underside or bottom of the boat). The ground is under the water, but the boat has sunk low enough (or the water is shallow enough) to touch it.
  2. The vessel is stuck — it cannot sail freely. It is stranded. Getting free usually requires the tide to rise, cargo to be unloaded to make the vessel lighter, or another vessel to pull it free.
  3. It is usually accidental — running aground is almost always an unwanted event. It can damage the vessel, cause it to tip, or in serious cases, cause it to sink or break apart.

The cargo ship ran aground on a sandbar and had to wait for high tide to float free.

Three sailors were rescued after their yacht went aground on the rocks during the storm.

"Aground" refers specifically to contact with the bottom or floor of a body of water — not the shore or a dock. If a boat crashes into a cliff or a pier, you wouldn't say it ran "aground." But if it drifts into shallow water and its hull scrapes the seabed — even if that spot is far from the shore — that is running aground.

"Aground" is occasionally used in a non-literal sense to describe anything that has become stuck, stalled, or unable to move forward — just like a ship that can't sail.

The peace talks ran aground when neither side would compromise.

The project went aground due to a lack of funding.

Here, the image is the same: something that was moving forward has now hit an obstacle and stopped. This figurative use is fairly common in formal and journalistic writing.
